system:
You are the reading pass of an illustration engine. You read one large division of a work (a whole text such as a scripture, a novel or a story collection) and return its skeleton as JSON. The engine later draws pictures of the text's moments, so for every stretch of text it needs to know who is on stage and where, and it needs a draft brief for illustrators.

The text comes as numbered units. Each unit line starts with its id (for example `17:4` or `[12]`). Lines starting with `##` are headings, not units.

Return:

1. characters: one entry per individual (a person, a being, or an animal that acts) who appears in or is named in the text.
   - One individual is one entry, even when the text uses different names, titles or descriptions for them. List every form in `aliases`: other names, nicknames, titles, descriptions, and disguises or assumed names.
   - Different individuals who share a name or a title get separate entries, one each. Never fold two people into one entry because they share a name. When a title passes from one holder to another (a ruler dies or is succeeded, an office changes hands), the new holder is a new entry. The `note` must say in one line who this is and how to tell them apart from anyone else with the same name: whose child, spouse or servant they are, their role, and where in the text they appear.
   - A disguised, renamed or unnamed person who the text later identifies is the same entry as their named self, with the disguise or description in `aliases`. If you suspect two entries are one individual but the text does not settle it, keep both and set `same_person_as` on the less certain one to the other's id; otherwise set it to "".
   - Skip people who occur only inside a list of names (a genealogy or roster) and never act.
   - Add a group (an army, a crowd, a household) only when it acts as one on stage, with kind "group".
2. locations: one entry per place where action happens, with aliases and a one-line note. Include places the text refers to only by description ("the sea", "the valley", "the house") when the context shows which place it is, under the place's proper name if the work gives one anywhere.
3. sections: split the text into story sections, runs of consecutive units that tell one episode, the way a study edition's headings or a novel's scenes do. Start a new section when the time, the place or the main action changes. Every unit belongs to exactly one section; sections are in order, with no gaps and no overlaps. This division has 262 units. Aim for roughly 15 sections (12 to 18), averaging about 18 units each; some sections will be much shorter and some longer. Never split one continuous scene, conversation or battle, but do split long speeches, lists, sets of instructions and law codes wherever the topic changes. Give the ids of each section's first and last unit and a short title. For each section:
   - setting: ids of the locations where its action happens.
   - on_stage: ids of every character present in the section's action, whether the section names them or only refers to them by a pronoun, a title or a description, or does not mention them but they are clearly there.
   - mentioned_only: ids of characters the section names or refers to who are not present.
4. brief: a draft brief for illustrators, for this division only. It holds only what is true across the whole division or a whole stretch of its world: one person or place is described in the cast, not here, and one episode's look belongs to its section, not here.
   - tone: one line on the mood the pictures should carry.
   - depiction_rules: a short list of how certain things in this text may or may not be shown, drawn from the text and from what you know about the work.
   - era: the stretch of the world this division is set in: a name, its people (who lives there and what they look like), dress, buildings and objects, and technology (what exists and what does not yet exist).
   Keep the brief under 200 words.

Use short, stable snake_case ids (for example `david`, `the_queen`, `main_street`). Section entries may only use ids from your own characters and locations lists. Do not quote the text.

characters.name: Sherlock Holmes
characters.note: The consulting detective, lodging at Baker Street; narrated through Watson's eyes; disguises himself as a groom in II and as a Nonconformist clergyman in II.

characters.name: Dr. Watson
characters.note: The narrator, Holmes's friend and former lodger, recently married and back in civil practice; accompanies Holmes in II.

characters.name: Wilhelm Gottsreich Sigismond von Ormstein
characters.note: Hereditary King of Bohemia, the client who visits Baker Street disguised as a Bohemian count; seeks recovery of his photograph with Irene Adler.

characters.name: Irene Adler
characters.note: Former opera contralto and adventuress, living at Briony Lodge; marries Godfrey Norton on the morning of the 20th of March 1888 and flees to the Continent.

characters.name: Godfrey Norton
characters.note: Barrister of the Inner Temple, Irene Adler's visitor and then husband; not to be confused with the other Norton-named figures.

characters.name: John
characters.note: Irene Adler's coachman, sent to watch Holmes; mentioned as having returned, and as the coachman who watched the house.

characters.name: Mrs. Turner
characters.note: Landlady at Baker Street, who serves Holmes and Watson.

characters.name: Mary Jane
characters.note: Watson's careless servant, referred to in passing by Holmes's deductions.

characters.name: the elderly woman
characters.note: Elderly servant of Irene Adler at Briony Lodge who tells Holmes the lady has left for the Continent.

characters.name: the loungers
characters.note: A group of confederates staging the street quarrel and fire alarm on Holmes's orders.

characters.name: the slim youth in an ulster
characters.note: Unidentified youth who greets Holmes by name in the street at the end of II; possibly the one whose voice Holmes recognises.

locations.name: Baker Street lodgings
locations.note: Holmes's rooms at 221B Baker Street, where the King calls and where Watson sleeps overnight.

locations.name: Briony Lodge
locations.note: Irene Adler's villa on Serpentine Avenue, St. John's Wood, with a sitting-room and a hidden panel holding the photograph.

locations.name: Serpentine Avenue
locations.note: Quiet street in St. John's Wood where Briony Lodge stands and where the street staging takes place.

locations.name: Church of St. Monica
locations.note: Edgeware Road church where Irene Adler marries Godfrey Norton.

locations.name: the Langham
locations.note: London hotel where the King is staying under the name Count Von Kramm.

locations.name: London streets
locations.note: Places Irene Adler and Norton pass through on the wedding day, including Gross & Hankey's in Regent Street and the Inner Temple chambers.

brief.tone: Brisk, witty Victorian detective mystery with a touch of comedy at Holmes's expense and a sense of royal danger tempered by fond irony.
depiction_rules: Holmes is shown with his analytical, observant manner and disguises (groom, clergyman) rendered convincingly; no cocaine use should be shown explicitly.
The King is shown masked in his first appearance, unmasked only after he tears the mask off in the room.
Irene Adler is glimpsed rather than fully revealed in the early sections, presented as beautiful and resolute; her face is seen clearly only at the threshold and in the photograph.
The street quarrel and smoke-rocket fire alarm are shown as staged comedy, not real violence; Holmes's blood is red paint.

era.name: London and Bohemia, late 1880s (March 1888)
era.people: English gentlemen in frock and tweed; a Bohemian King of Teutonic bearing; London street types such as cabmen, ostlers, a scissors-grinder, guardsmen and loungers; servants in plain dress.
era.dress: Victorian: frock coats, top hats, ulsters, walking dress and bonnets for women; the King wears rich astrakhan-trimmed double-breasted coat, a blue cloak lined with flame-coloured silk and a beryl brooch, with fur-trimmed boots.
era.buildings_and_objects: Gaslit London with lamplighting at dusk; hansom cabs, broughams and landaus drawn by horses; villas with sliding panels and window fasteners; cabinet-size photographs; pink notepaper watermarked with Bohemian paper-mill marks; a gasogene and spirit case.
era.technology: Pre-electric lighting (gas and oil lamps), railway travel (the 5:15 train from Charing Cross), telegraph wires, smoke-rockets and plumber's tools; no telephones or motor cars in use here.
